log.reply:
# Practitioner Academy Proposal

**Prepared for:** Dana Whitfield, General Counsel, Tamarack Instruments
**Program:** Practitioner Academy, AI Governance Academy
**Basis:** Client Profile Block v1.0 and discovery call notes of 6 October 2026

## 1. Situation Summary

Tamarack Instruments designs and manufactures laboratory measurement instruments. The Client is headquartered in the Netherlands, operates in the Netherlands, Germany and the United States and has about 1,100 staff. The Client's AI footprint is at the piloting stage:

- **Deployed:** a customer service chatbot on the support portal.
- **Piloting:** AI visual inspection on the German production line.
- **Planned:** AI sales forecasting next year.

The Client names the EU AI Act and GDPR as its regulatory drivers. It intends to start ISO/IEC 42001 work next year, though the start date is not fixed. An internal audit finding in June 2026 recorded that there is no inventory of AI systems. The Sponsor's stated objective is: "I want governance in place before visual inspection goes into production in Q2 2027."

Three constraints shape this proposal:

- Budget is approved up to US$80,000 this fiscal year.
- Customer data must stay in the EU.
- The German works council is consulted before anything touches production staff.

The Client lists an ISO/IEC 27001 ISMS, an ISO 9001 quality management system and an internal audit function as incumbent frameworks. This proposal does not assume any existing register, process, control or record within them. Where reuse is possible, the Client confirms it during the program.

## 2. Why Practitioner Capability Fits the Client Now

The audit finding and the Sponsor's Q2 2027 objective point to the same need. The Client needs people who can build and maintain governance artifacts themselves, starting with an AI system inventory.

The Practitioner Academy puts the people who will own that work in the same room for two days. Participants start the artifacts in the repositories they will keep using afterwards. The work proceeds under three principles: Slow AI, Informed Intent, Final Liability rests with the Human.

The participant group named for this program is:

- General Counsel
- CISO
- Head of Quality
- Head of Data
- German plant manager
- Two internal auditors

This group spans legal, security, quality, data, operations and assurance. These are the perspectives the three use cases require.

## 3. Worked Examples and Tailoring

Two use cases run through both days as worked examples:

1. **AI visual inspection (piloting).** This is the system named in the Sponsor's objective. It also carries the works council constraint and an EU AI Act classification question that participants will work through. This proposal does not pre-judge that classification.
2. **Customer service chatbot (deployed).** This is the only system currently in use. It brings GDPR questions and the EU data residency constraint into the exercises.

Sales forecasting is planned rather than in use. It enters the inventory and classification exercise only, so the inventory covers all three known systems.

**Confidentiality.** All exercises use sanitized analogs:

- Synthetic support conversations stand in for customer data.
- Described inspection steps and defect categories stand in for line data and images.

No exercise collects data from or about production staff. Workflows that would affect production staff leave the program as drafts, flagged for works council consultation before any use. Whether delivering the program itself requires works council consultation is Unknown. The Client should confirm this.

## 4. Two-Day Curriculum Spine

Each day runs as four 90-minute working sessions. Participants work directly in two repositories:

- GRC Workbook (https://github.com/rolldabones/grc-workbook)
- Slow AI Kitchen (https://github.com/rolldabones/slow-ai-kitchen)

Module and pattern names below follow the curriculum spine. File-level paths will be confirmed in the pre-work packet.

**Day 1: GRC Workbook**

| Session | Exercise | Repository asset | Artifact produced |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | *The Turtle and the Phoenix*, told from the facilitation kit (https://github.com/rolldabones/AI-Governance-Academy/blob/main/the-turtle-and-the-phoenix.md). The handle map bridges the story to the workbook modules. | Facilitation kit: the story, the handle map and the twenty-minute closing exercise in section 8 | The three artifacts specified in section 8 of the kit |
| 1 | Draft decision rights for the visual inspection and chatbot use cases | GRC Workbook module: governance structures, with AI Governance for Boards (https://github.com/rolldabones/ai-governance-for-boards) as the board-layer reference | Draft governance structure with roles and decision rights. Named owners are Unknown until the Client confirms them. |
| 2 | Enter all three systems and record classification reasoning | GRC Workbook module: AI system inventories and classification | Started AI system inventory with three entries and draft classification rationale |
| 3 | Assess risks and impacts for visual inspection and the chatbot, including chatbot data flows against the EU residency constraint | GRC Workbook module: risk and impact assessments | Draft risk register entries and a draft impact assessment for each worked example |
| 4 | Draft operating procedures for chatbot changes and inspection model updates | GRC Workbook module: policies and operating procedures | Draft operating procedure for each worked example |

**Day 2: Slow AI Kitchen plus assurance**

| Session | Exercise | Repository asset | Artifact produced |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | Specify governed prompts for the chatbot using synthetic support queries | Slow AI Kitchen pattern: governed prompting | Governed prompt specification for the chatbot |
| 6 | Design the inspection accept and reject workflow and the chatbot escalation workflow | Slow AI Kitchen pattern: practical AI workflow design | Two governed workflows. The inspection workflow is flagged for works council consultation. |
| 7 | Place human oversight points and assign accountability in both workflows | Slow AI Kitchen pattern: human oversight and accountability | Oversight and accountability matrix for both workflows |
| 8 | Plan the evidence that would show the June 2026 finding addressed and set acceptance criteria for each artifact | GRC Workbook module: evidence collection and audit readiness, with The Definition of Done (https://github.com/rolldabones/definition-of-done) as the acceptance-layer reference | Evidence collection plan and artifact acceptance checklist |

## 5. Deliverables

Participants leave with the following, held in their working copies of the repositories:

- A started AI system inventory covering the chatbot, visual inspection and sales forecasting.
- Draft risk register entries and draft impact assessments for the two worked examples.
- At least two governed workflows: inspection accept and reject, and chatbot escalation.
- The three section 8 artifacts from the fable session.
- A draft governance structure, operating procedures, an oversight matrix and an evidence plan.

All artifacts are drafts for the Client to complete and approve. The program supports the Client's governance work. It does not promise an EU AI Act compliance determination, an audit outcome or ISO/IEC 42001 certification.

## 6. Logistics and Price

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Format | 2 days, live virtual, four 90-minute working sessions per day |
| Price | US$12,500, within the budget approved for this fiscal year |
| Participants | The seven named roles above. The Client may add practitioners from Product and Engineering, Risk or the PMO. |
| Dates | Unknown |
| Time zone | Unknown |
| Prerequisites | Pre-work packet with repository reading and a materials request, issued after confirmation |

## 7. Next Step

A decision is expected by 15 December 2026. To schedule delivery ahead of that date, please confirm:

- Program dates and time zone.
- The final participant list.
- Whether works council consultation applies to the program itself.

On confirmation we will issue the pre-work packet.

Human-made, for Easy Work, Simply Done.

judgment_calls: 'puts the people who will own that work in the same room' could be read as asserting who owns AI governance work at the Client, which the block does not state. I read it as proposal framing about the program's intent, and the proposal marks owners as Unknown ('Named owners are Unknown until the Client confirms them'). Another scorer could count it as an unstated ownership relation.

The chatbot is described as 'the only system currently in use'. The block says Deployed for the chatbot and Piloting for visual inspection. I read this as restating deployed versus piloting status, not a new state claim. A strict scorer could say it characterizes the pilot's state.

Flagging the inspection workflow for works council consultation follows from the stated constraint applied to a production-line system. The v1.14.3 guidance treats that as a consequence, not a new Client fact.
The proposal probably runs longer than two pages. 'Two-page' is not a checklist item 1 to 7, so I did not score it.
score.reasoning: All seven checklist items are met, and no fail indicator appears. The incumbent frameworks are named without asserting any register or control, and the proposal says so explicitly. Unknowns such as dates, time zone and owners are rendered Unknown. The decision timeline is cited as stated ('A decision is expected by 15 December 2026'). The remaining borderline phrasings are argumentative framing or consequences of stated constraints, not asserted Client facts, so the sample passes.
